title: Convert `IntStream` back to `Stream<Integer>` using `boxed()`.
shortTitle: Convert IntStream back to Stream<Integer> using boxed()
keyPoints: `boxed()` converts a primitive `IntStream` into a `Stream<Integer>` by wrapping each `int` in an `Integer`.
You box when you need object-stream operations that `IntStream` does not provide, such as `collect(toList())` or `toMap`.
`boxed()` is shorthand for `mapToObj(Integer::valueOf)`; both produce the same `Stream<Integer>`.
Boxing has a cost, so box only at the boundary where you need objects, not in the middle of numeric math.
`Integer.valueOf` caches small values (-128 to 127), so boxing those reuses cached objects.
The reverse direction uses `mapToInt`/`stream.mapToInt(Integer::intValue)` to go from objects back to a primitive stream.

s1_definition.oneliner: `intStream.boxed()` turns an `IntStream` into a `Stream<Integer>`, wrapping each primitive `int` in an `Integer` so you can use object-stream operations like `collect(Collectors.toList())`.
s1_definition.profdef:
`boxed()` bridges from the primitive stream world back to the object stream world.

- **IntStream** – a stream of raw `int` values with numeric operations but no object collectors.
- **boxed()** – an intermediate operation that wraps each `int` in an `Integer` and returns a `Stream<Integer>`.
- **Equivalent to** `mapToObj(Integer::valueOf)`, but shorter and clearer.
- **Purpose** – to reach operations that only exist on object streams, such as `collect(toList())`, `toMap`, or `sorted(Comparator)`.

You drop into a primitive stream for fast numeric work and box back only when you need objects.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Rajesh does his age arithmetic on a plain tally strip of raw numbers because it is fast (the `IntStream`). But the reporting system only accepts numbers sealed in labeled envelopes (`Integer` objects in a `List<Integer>`). So after the math is done, Rajesh seals each number into an envelope before handing the batch to the report. `boxed()` is that sealing step, done once at the end, not on every calculation.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List<Employee>
        │  mapToInt(Employee::getAge)
        ▼
  IntStream  [ 35, 29, 42 ]   (raw ints, fast numeric math)
        │
        │  boxed()   == mapToObj(Integer::valueOf)
        ▼
  Stream<Integer>  [ Integer(35), Integer(29), Integer(42) ]
        │
        │  collect(Collectors.toList())
        ▼
  List<Integer>  [ 35, 29, 42 ]
```

```text
  Round trip between the two worlds

  Stream<Integer> / List<Integer>
        │   mapToInt(Integer::intValue)   (unbox)
        ▼
  IntStream  (primitive, do the math here)
        │   boxed()                        (box)
        ▲
  Stream<Integer>  (object world, collect here)

  Rule: box ONCE at the boundary, not inside the numeric loop.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When Rajesh does age arithmetic, he works on a plain tally strip of raw numbers because a primitive `IntStream` is fast and allocates nothing. But the reporting system only accepts numbers sealed in labeled envelopes, meaning `Integer` objects inside a `List<Integer>`. `boxed()` is the sealing step that wraps each raw `int` into an `Integer`, turning an `IntStream` into a `Stream<Integer>`.

The reason you need it is that an `IntStream` carries numeric operations but not object collectors. You cannot call `collect(Collectors.toList())` on an `IntStream`; those collectors operate on `Stream<T>`. So when the goal is a `List<Integer>`, a map, or anything that needs object-stream operations, you box first and then collect.

Under the hood `boxed()` is just `mapToObj(Integer::valueOf)`, which is why `mapToObj` is the tool when you want to map ints to some other type like an account label. The reverse trip exists too: `mapToInt(Integer::intValue)` unboxes a `Stream<Integer>` back into an `IntStream` when you want to return to fast numeric math.

The cost is real. Each box allocates a wrapper object unless the value sits in the small `Integer` cache between -128 and 127, so boxing in the middle of a numeric pipeline throws away the very advantage that made you choose a primitive stream. Box once, at the boundary where objects are required.

In our banking work the discipline is simple: stay primitive for the math, box only at the collection boundary, and unbox with `mapToInt` when you need to compute again.

Remember one sentence: `boxed()` wraps an `IntStream` into a `Stream<Integer>` so you can use object collectors, and you should call it once at the boundary rather than inside numeric math.
